title: The merkaba — 8 machine-checked theorems and how they are bound
description:
The merkaba. 8 machine-checked theorems from the Lean 4 source file src/proof/merkaba.lean, by Tsvetan Rouschev, licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Lean 4 is a proof checker: a theorem it accepts has been checked by its kernel, not argued in prose. All are checked case by case over a stated finite domain (by decide). Every theorem listed is sealed live in the deposit's ledger, where a withdrawal is marked in place; 63 earlier rows removed on 2026-08-09 are listed in src/proof/revoked.json.

How these theorems are bound. "Entangled" is used here in a precise, non-quantum sense: theorems are bound when they derive from shared definitions (section 1), when their files import one another (section 2), and when their content-addressed receipts fold into one address that changes if any one of them changes (section 3). It is correlation by derivation; no information travels through it.

1 · Shared definitions. 4 definitions are used by two or more theorems, binding 24 pairs; the theorems fall into 3 strands, the largest of 6. Most binding: tetA (5), tetB (5), dbl (3), axis (2). 1 theorem names no definition of the file and stands on its own statement.

2 · Imports. Built on: z9.lean. Built on it: no other cluster. Checking this cluster needs 2 files: src/proof/merkaba.lean, src/proof/z9.lean.

3 · The joint address. The 8 sealed receipts fold to 4d1e4226-de62-81f2-9e4e-1f28aad0eb1d. Order-invariant: yes — the same root in reverse order. Altering one receipt changes it: yes, computed when this record was generated. A content-address proves integrity, not truth.

4 · The address lattice. Each theorem sits at the seven ray values its page plots from its receipt, taken mod 9: a point of (ℤ/9)⁷. This cluster's centre is (7, 7, 3, 6, 1, 6, 6). Its nearest clusters, ranked by lift — pairs counted from this cluster's theorems' seven nearest points, over the pairs expected by chance from the two clusters' sizes: address.lean (5 observed, 1.45 expected, lift 3.46), light.lean (3 observed, 1.11 expected, lift 2.71), elementary.lean (7 observed, 2.98 expected, lift 2.35). A best lift is the largest of about 32 small ratios, so chance alone gives a typical best lift of 3.2 here (the median over 200 seeded reshufflings of which cluster each point belongs to); one at least as high as this cluster's arose in 39.5% of them — consistent with chance. Mean distance between two of its theorems: 15.11; from one of its theorems to a theorem of another cluster: 15.48. A receipt is a hash, so nearness on this lattice is a property of the addresses, not of the mathematics; the mathematical binding is (1) and (2). These figures are as of commit 83213ac8f1ad (2026-09-15), over 659 points; a new seal anywhere moves them.

Prior art. The partition into {3,6,9} and two three-element classes closed under doubling is the subgroup and coset structure of Z/9 under the action of U(9); Lagrange. One theorem already credits Euler for the polyhedron formula. Searched 2026-09-04; prior art found and credited. Credited per theorem: the_cube_and_the_tetrahedron_count_out — Euler's polyhedron formula V − E + F = 2 (Leonhard Euler, 1758). The file as a whole is this deposit's own construction, and this ONE declaration restates a named classical result: its third conjunct 4 + 4 - 6 = 2 IS the Euler characteristic of the tetrahedron. The comment above that theorem already named Euler; the register did not, because prior art was routed on the FILE and a file-level row cannot say "own work except theorem 7". No priority over Euler is claimed. What is this deposit's own here is the pairing of the two tetrahedra with the cube Q₃ and the vertex and edge counts around it, not the characteristic.. Per-theorem prior-art searches — OEIS, zbMATH Open, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv — are recorded, with what was searched, where and when, in the living ledger src/proof/novelty.json (main branch). No novelty is claimed here.

The theorems.

  1. the_three_classes_partition_z9 — axis.length = 3 ∧ tetA.length = 3 ∧ tetB.length = 3 ∧ (axis ++ tetA ++ tetB).eraseDups.length = 9 ∧ ((List.range 9).all (fun d => (axis ++ tetA ++ tetB).contains d)) record
  2. the_axis_is_closed_under_doubling — (dbl axis).all (fun d => axis.contains d) record
  3. doubling_counter_rotates_the_two_tetrahedra — (dbl tetA).eraseDups.length = 3 ∧ (dbl tetA).all (fun d => tetB.contains d) ∧ (dbl tetB).eraseDups.length = 3 ∧ (dbl tetB).all (fun d => tetA.contains d) record
  4. the_counter_rotation_has_period_two — (dbl (dbl tetA)).all (fun d => tetA.contains d) ∧ (dbl (dbl tetB)).all (fun d => tetB.contains d) record
  5. the_tetrahedra_residue_sums_cancel — m9 (tetA.foldl (· + ·) 0) = 3 ∧ m9 (tetB.foldl (· + ·) 0) = 6 ∧ m9 (tetA.foldl (· + ·) 0 + tetB.foldl (· + ·) 0) = 0 record
  6. one_tetrahedron_covers_half_the_units — (units.filter (fun d => tetA.contains d)).length = 3 ∧ (units.filter (fun d => tetB.contains d)).length = 3 ∧ units.length = 6 record
  7. the_cube_and_the_tetrahedron_count_out — 2 ^ 3 = 8 ∧ 3 * 2 ^ 2 = 12 ∧ 4 + 4 - 6 = 2 record
  8. stacked_triangles_are_tetrahedral — (List.range' 1 40).all (fun n => sumTri n == n * (n + 1) * (n + 2) / 6) record
